## Important Points
::: { .r-stack}
::: {.fragment .absolute .fade-out data-fragment-index="1"}

+ Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) is the general category comprising the following systems:
    + GPS: United States, first satellite launched in 1978
    + GLONASS: Russia/Soviet Union, first satellite launched in 1982
    + BeiDou: China, first satellite launched in 2000
    + Galileo: European Union, first test satellite launched in 2005

:::

::: {.fragment .absolute .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="1"}

+ Signals from Satellites
    + Signals contain the position of the satellite, and the exact time sent
    + $\ell = c t$

:::

::: {.fragment .absolute .fade-in-then-out style="font-size:0.7em" data-fragment-index="2"}


If you know your distance from 3 points in 3D space, theoretically you know where you are, 

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{(x - x_1)^{2} + (y - y_1)^{2} + (z - z_1)^{2}} = c t_1\\
\sqrt{(x - x_2)^{2} + (y - y_2)^{2} + (z - z_2)^{2}} = c t_2\\
\sqrt{(x - x_3)^{2} + (y - y_3)^{2} + (z - z_3)^{2}} = c t_3
\end{aligned}
$$

but __there are sources of error__ ...

:::

::: {.fragment .absolute .fade-in-then-out style="font-size:0.7em" data-fragment-index="3"}
Your the ground unit's time is wrong, so you need at tleast 4 satellites to solve for distance error caused by clock error, _b_.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{(x - x_1)^{2} + (y - y_1)^{2} + (z - z_1)^{2}} = c t_1 + b\\
\sqrt{(x - x_2)^{2} + (y - y_2)^{2} + (z - z_2)^{2}} = c t_2 + b\\
\sqrt{(x - x_3)^{2} + (y - y_3)^{2} + (z - z_3)^{2}} = c t_3 + b\\
\sqrt{(x - x_4)^{2} + (y - y_4)^{2} + (z - z_4)^{2}} = c t_4 + b
\end{aligned}
$$

:::

::: {.fragment .absolute .fade-in-then-out style="font-size:0.7em" data-fragment-index="4"}

+ How does the satellite know where it is?
    + Ground stations!
+ How do the ground stations know where they are, what with the continents moving around and all?
    + Qulsars!
    + Radio telescopes male a precise map of continental movement from qulsars
    + Ground stations are tied into that map

:::

::: {.fragment .absolute .fade-in-then-out style="font-size:0.7em" data-fragment-index="5"}

+ Other complexities:
    + Relativistic effects
    + Rotation of earth
    + Atmospheric effects

+ So GNSS units use many satellites to improve location
    + phones, ~ 3m
    + Precision units , cms

::: 

::: {.fragment .absolute .fade-in-then-out style="font-size:0.7em" data-fragment-index="6"}

+ GPS signals are weak
    + transmitted at about 50 W
    + arrives at about $10^{-16}$ W

:::

::: {.fragment .absolute .fade-in-then-out style="font-size:0.7em" data-fragment-index="7"}

Here’s a slide-friendly table. These are **carrier center frequencies** in **MHz**.

| System | Operator | Main GNSS signals | Frequencies |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| **GPS** | U.S. | L1, L2, L5 | 1575.42, 1227.60, 1176.45 |
| **Galileo** | European Union | E1, E5a, E5b, E5, E6 | 1575.42, 1176.45, 1207.14, 1191.795, 1278.75 |
| **BeiDou** | China | B1I, B1C, B2a, B2b/B2I, B3I | 1561.098, 1575.42, 1176.45, 1207.14, 1268.52 |
| **GLONASS** | Russia | L1, L2 | L1: 1598.0625-1605.375; L2: 1242.9375-1248.625 |
| **QZSS** | Japan | L1, L2, L5, L6 | 1575.42, 1227.60, 1176.45, 1278.75 |
| **NavIC** | India | L1, L5, S-band | 1575.42, 1176.45, 2492.028 |

Note: **GLONASS is different** because its older signals use slightly different frequencies for different satellites, so it is listed as ranges.

Sources: [GPS.gov](https://archive.gps.gov/systems/gps/modernization/civilsignals/), [ESA/Galileo Navipedia](https://gssc.esa.int/navipedia/index.php/GALILEO_Signal_Plan), [BeiDou CSNO/TARC](https://www.csno-tarc.cn/status/introductionEn?lang=en), [GLONASS ICD listing](https://jsapt.net/ja/post/08120001), [QZSS Cabinet Office](https://qzss.go.jp/en/overview/services/sv03_signals.html), [ISRO NavIC FAQ](https://www.isro.gov.in/ISRO_EN/FAQ_Applications.html).

:::

## Exercise

::: { .r-stack}

::: {.fragment .absolute style="font-size:0.6em" .fade-out data-fragment-index="1"}

__Drain scavenger hunt__

+ Work in pairs and find storm drains around campus
+ For each drain, take one clear photo
+ Use your phone to record the latitude and longitude in decimal degrees

+ For each drain, enter the following into the Google Form:
    + latitude
    + longitude
    + approximate size in cm
    + shape: round, rectangular, or other
    + photo
    
:::

::: {.fragment .absolute style="font-size:0.7em" .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="1"}

+ After the class has submitted data:
    + open the linked Google Sheet
    + download the sheet as a CSV
    + open QGIS
    + add the CSV as a delimited text layer
    + set X field = longitude and Y field = latitude
    + set the CRS to WGS84, EPSG:4326
    + inspect the points and fix any obvious coordinate errors


:::

::: {.fragment .absolute .fade-in-then-out style="font-size:0.7em" data-fragment-index="2"}

+ Add photo locations from EXIF data:
    + download the original uploaded photos from Google Drive
    + in QGIS, open the Processing Toolbox
    + search for and run `Import geotagged photos`
    + use the downloaded photo folder as the input folder
    + create a point layer from the photo EXIF coordinates
    + compare the EXIF photo points to the manually entered CSV points
    + note which photos are missing location data or plot in the wrong place

:::

:::
